video.title: 9 One-Person Businesses With More Demand Than Competition

summary: The host ranks nine businesses he says have more demand than professional competition, from portable sanitation to remote cleaning. The examples range from physical route services and skilled trades to recruiting and service businesses coordinated remotely. He favors recurring revenue and businesses where contractors do the physical work while the owner handles sales and operations. His top pick is remote cleaning, which he promotes alongside his training and one-to-one business support.

speakers.name: Host (name not stated)
speakers.description: First-person presenter on the Johnny & Sergio channel.

ideas.name: Portable sanitation rental and servicing
ideas.one_liner: Rent portable toilets to construction sites and events, then service and restock them.
ideas.business_model: Recurring monthly per-unit rental and service contracts, plus short event rentals.
ideas.customer: Construction sites, weddings, festivals, and other outdoor events.
ideas.problem: Construction sites need on-site sanitation, and outdoor events need temporary facilities.
ideas.offer: Place portable sanitation units and pump them out and restock them on a service schedule.

pricing.model: Monthly per-unit contracts for construction and short-term rentals for events.

ideas.delivery: The owner or crew transports and places units, drives between sites, pumps out waste, and restocks supplies.
unit_economics_claims: Construction contracts may last 6–18 months, with monthly per-unit billing and weekly service.
A hypothetical job with 20 units would create a recurring monthly revenue base; no amount is stated.
ideas.startup_cost: Requires upfront capital to purchase units; amount not stated.

acquisition.how: Site and event sales are not described as software-led; a person would likely need to arrange contracts.

onboarding.how: Contract details and unit placement could be scheduled with software, but site requirements need human coordination.

delivery.how: People must transport, place, pump, and restock the physical units.

billing.how: Recurring per-unit invoicing could be automated once contracts and service records are set up.

support.how: Routine scheduling can be handled with software, but missed service or site issues need human follow-up.

uk_applicability.notes: Construction and outdoor events also need temporary sanitation in the UK. Local waste handling, site, and event requirements would need to be followed.

risks: The business needs substantial upfront asset capital.
Pumping, restocking, driving, and placement are physical work.
Service reliability matters across dispersed sites.

quotes.text: Every active construction site is legally required to have sanitation on site for the entire length of the build.
quotes.speaker: Host (name not stated)

ideas.name: Small engine repair
ideas.one_liner: Repair engines in contractor and household equipment such as mowers, generators, and pressure washers.
ideas.business_model: Paid repair work; exact charging model is not stated.
ideas.customer: Landscaping crews, contractors, and households with small-engine equipment.
ideas.problem: Specialized equipment breaks down, and owners may struggle to find a responsive, reliable repair shop.
ideas.offer: Provide fast, dependable small-engine diagnosis and repair from an accessible shop.

pricing.model: Repair fees; details are not stated.

ideas.delivery: A skilled mechanic diagnoses and repairs customers' equipment at a shop. The host emphasizes fast turnaround and same-day callbacks.
unit_economics_claims: The host describes the business as capable of producing strong dollars per hour, but gives no figures.
ideas.startup_cost: Shop and equipment costs are not stated.

acquisition.how: A website and listing could generate inbound enquiries, but no acquisition method is described and the service depends on local trust.

onboarding.how: Intake forms and booking can be automated, but a person must assess the equipment and repair needs.

delivery.how: A skilled mechanic must diagnose and repair each physical machine.

billing.how: Invoices and payment reminders can be automated after a mechanic records the job.

support.how: Automated updates can cover routine status checks, but repair questions and callbacks need human attention.

uk_applicability.notes: The equipment and contractor demand described are also relevant in the UK; local demand and seasonality will vary.

risks: The trade takes time to learn.
Repair work requires human labor.
Demand can be seasonal, especially when outdoor contractors have less work in winter.
Fast turnaround and reliable callbacks are central to the proposed advantage.

quotes.text: if you can do all of that, then all of that demand is yours.
quotes.speaker: Host (name not stated)

ideas.name: Fire extinguisher testing and servicing
ideas.one_liner: Inspect and service fire extinguishers for commercial buildings on a recurring schedule.
ideas.business_model: Recurring annual inspections and service for commercial accounts.
ideas.customer: Offices, restaurants, warehouses, apartment buildings, and other businesses with fire extinguishers.
ideas.problem: Businesses need their extinguishers inspected on schedule and may face consequences if they are not compliant.
ideas.offer: Inspect extinguishers and attach the service tag, then return on the building's inspection schedule.

pricing.model: Inspection and servicing fees; exact model and prices are not stated.
pricing.notes: The host describes recurring business but gives no price.

ideas.delivery: An inspector visits buildings, checks extinguishers, and attaches service tags. The host describes repeat annual visits.
unit_economics_claims: The host says a route of a few hundred accounts can add substantial recurring revenue.
He says fire inspection businesses can reach millions or tens of millions in annual revenue, without identifying specific operators.
ideas.time_to_first_revenue: Not stated; the host says building a route takes time because commercial sales cycles are long.

acquisition.how: The compliance need can motivate buyers, but the host says commercial selling takes time and gives no automated acquisition method.

onboarding.how: Building records and inspection dates can be stored in software, but site details need human review.

delivery.how: An inspector must physically check extinguishers and attach tags.

billing.how: Recurring account billing and annual reminders could be automated once the route is established.

support.how: Routine reminders can be automated, but compliance questions and inspection exceptions need a qualified person.

uk_applicability.notes: The recurring inspection need is relevant in the UK, but the host's legal and inspection claims concern the US. UK requirements and competence standards would need to be checked.

risks: The service is not described as high-ticket, so building a large route may be necessary.
Commercial sales cycles can be long.
The legal and inspection requirements described are US-specific and should not be assumed to apply unchanged in the UK.

quotes.text: once you get in with, you know, a building's annual inspection schedule, you're back every single year, tag after tag.
quotes.speaker: Host (name not stated)

ideas.name: Commercial dock and door equipment service
ideas.one_liner: Repair and maintain loading dock equipment, including dock levers, roll-up doors, and dock seals.
ideas.business_model: Quarterly preventive maintenance contracts plus emergency repair calls.
ideas.customer: Warehouses, distribution centers, grocery loading docks, and other operators with loading bays.
ideas.problem: Dock equipment is heavily used and failures can stop a warehouse from loading or unloading trucks.
ideas.offer: Inspect and maintain dock equipment, then provide urgent repair when a bay fails.

pricing.model: Quarterly service visits and emergency repair charges.

price_points.label: a few hundred dollars per visit

pricing.notes: The visit price is presented as an example; emergency rates are described only as premium.

ideas.delivery: A technician diagnoses and repairs equipment at warehouses. The work involves electrical, hydraulic, motor, sensor, and safety systems.
unit_economics_claims: A hypothetical 20-account quarterly service route at a few hundred dollars per visit would produce recurring revenue, before emergency calls.

acquisition.how: Inbound marketing could generate enquiries, but no specific channel is described and commercial accounts may require direct sales.

onboarding.how: Asset inventories and maintenance schedules can be recorded in software, but equipment condition requires human inspection.

delivery.how: A skilled technician must physically inspect, diagnose, and repair the equipment.

billing.how: Quarterly contract invoicing can be automated; emergency jobs still need job records and approval.

support.how: Software can route service requests, but equipment breakdowns require a technician to respond.

uk_applicability.notes: Warehouses and loading docks are common in the UK too. Local electrical, equipment safety, and training requirements may differ.

risks: The work requires electrical and hydraulic knowledge.
The host says the equipment can be dangerous.
The core diagnosis and repair work cannot be automated away.

quotes.text: So, when a bay goes down, that warehouse can't load or unload trucks.
quotes.speaker: Host (name not stated)

ideas.name: Waste oil collection and recycling
ideas.one_liner: Collect used oil and grease from businesses, charge for pickup, and resell oil to re-refiners.
ideas.business_model: Recurring pickup fees plus resale of collected oil.
ideas.customer: Auto shops, restaurants producing fryer grease, and small manufacturers.
ideas.problem: Businesses need their oil and grease removed and recycled rather than discarded improperly.
ideas.offer: Collect oil on a recurring schedule and sell used oil to re-refiners.

pricing.model: Pickup fee plus potential resale proceeds from collected oil.
pricing.notes: No pickup fees or resale prices are stated.

ideas.delivery: The operator uses a vacuum truck to collect oil and grease from customer sites and transports it for recycling or resale.
unit_economics_claims: The host describes two potential revenue streams from the same pickup route but gives no amounts.
ideas.startup_cost: Requires a vacuum truck and permits; the host says the startup cost is substantial but gives no amount.

acquisition.how: A company could attract inbound commercial enquiries, but the host does not describe an acquisition channel.

onboarding.how: Pickup schedules and account records could be managed in software, but site setup and waste details need human review.

delivery.how: A driver must operate the vacuum truck and collect physical waste.

billing.how: Recurring pickup invoices could be automated; resale accounting would need commodity and quantity records.

support.how: Routine schedule messages can be automated, but missed pickups and compliance issues need human attention.

uk_applicability.notes: The waste collection and recycling model could apply in the UK, but the required permits, waste handling rules, and resale market would need to be checked locally.

risks: A vacuum truck and permits require substantial startup capital.
The host says resale revenue moves with oil prices.
Collection, transport, and handling are physical operations.
The host's regulatory claims are not specific to UK rules.

quotes.text: So you can charge the pickup fee, right? But on top of this, you can also take that oil and sell it to re-refiners.
quotes.speaker: Host (name not stated)

ideas.name: Truck driver recruiting
ideas.one_liner: Use paid social ads to find qualified drivers and place them with trucking companies for a placement fee.
ideas.business_model: Success-based placement fees paid when a driver is hired and stays on.
ideas.customer: Trucking carriers that need qualified drivers.
ideas.problem: An unfilled truck costs carriers money, and they need a dependable flow of qualified drivers.
ideas.offer: Generate driver applicants, verify their CDL, record, and experience, then refer qualified candidates to carriers.

pricing.model: Placement fee per qualified driver hired and retained.
pricing.notes: The fee is reported second-hand as an upper limit. The host's example uses half that amount.

acquisition_channels.details: Run Facebook ads targeting CDL holders and owner-operators looking for better freight, higher earnings, or routes closer to home.

quote.text: All you need to learn how to do is run Facebook ads targeting CDL holders and owner-operators who are looking for better freight
quote.speaker: Host (name not stated)

ideas.delivery: The recruiter runs ads, checks candidates' CDL, driving record, and experience, and refers suitable candidates to trucking companies.
unit_economics_claims: A person the host spoke with said carriers lose about $4,000 per month for each truck without a qualified driver.
A hypothetical 10 placements per month at about half the stated maximum fee would generate about $20,000 per month.
ideas.startup_cost: The host says the main out-of-pocket cost is ad spend; amount not stated.

acquisition.how: Paid social campaigns and lead forms can be automated, with routine human checks needed to manage ad quality.

onboarding.how: Applications and document collection can be automated, but identity and qualification checks need human review.

delivery.how: Matching can be software-assisted, but verifying qualifications and securing a hire require human judgment.

billing.how: A placement invoice can be triggered by recorded hire and retention milestones, with human verification.

support.how: Automated updates can handle routine questions, but applicants and carriers may need direct help.

uk_applicability.notes: Recruiting could be adapted to UK haulage, but the US CDL references and carrier context do not transfer directly. UK driver qualifications, platforms, and hiring practices differ.

risks: This is a placement business rather than a subscription, so the pipeline must be replenished continually.
Revenue can be uneven if hiring slows or the pipeline thins.
Candidates must be properly checked before referral.
The host's claim about placement fees and carrier losses is second-hand.

quotes.text: You do have to make sure they have a valid CDL, clean record, and actual experience before you can hand them over
quotes.speaker: Host (name not stated)

ideas.name: Non-emergency medical transportation
ideas.one_liner: Coordinate rides to medical appointments by scheduling independent drivers and billing insurers or Medicaid.
ideas.business_model: Recurring rides billed to Medicaid or insurance, with independent drivers fulfilling trips.
ideas.customer: People who cannot drive themselves to dialysis, chemotherapy, or other medical appointments; payers include Medicaid and insurance plans.
ideas.problem: Some patients need repeated transportation to medical appointments and cannot drive themselves.
ideas.offer: Schedule rides, handle insurance billing and compliance, and route trips to independent drivers with suitable vehicles.

pricing.model: Ride charges billed to Medicaid or insurance; exact rates are not stated.
pricing.notes: The host says insurance billing can allow higher prices than consumer ride-hailing, but gives no amounts.

ideas.delivery: The operator schedules rides and routes them to independent drivers with wheelchair-accessible or standard vehicles. Drivers physically transport patients.
unit_economics_claims: A hypothetical dialysis patient could need three rides each week for years, creating repeat demand.
No trip rates or margins are stated.
ideas.startup_cost: Not stated; the host emphasizes paperwork and patience to set up insurance billing.
ideas.time_to_first_revenue: Not stated; the host says insurance payment can take time.

acquisition.how: No acquisition channel is described; trust and relationships around patient care are likely to require human involvement.

onboarding.how: Forms and ride preferences could be collected digitally, but eligibility and compliance records require careful review.

delivery.how: Drivers must physically pick up and transport patients reliably.

billing.how: Claims processing can be software-assisted, but payer rules, paperwork, and denials require human oversight.

support.how: Patients and case managers need reliable help with delays, changes, and driver issues.

uk_applicability.notes: Patient transport is relevant in the UK, but Medicaid is US-specific. The payer, commissioning, compliance, and billing arrangements would need substantial adaptation.

risks: Setting up Medicaid and managed-care billing involves substantial paperwork and patience.
Insurance payments may be slow.
Driver reliability directly affects patient experience and repeat business.
The work depends on drivers physically showing up on time.

quotes.text: You know, they are your product. So, if you're just sending out crap driver, your patients aren't going to want to keep booking
quotes.speaker: Host (name not stated)

ideas.name: Foundation repair and waterproofing lead coordination
ideas.one_liner: Generate and handle homeowner leads, inspections, and sales, then pass jobs to specialist repair crews for a share.
ideas.business_model: Commission or revenue share on one-off jobs completed by partner crews.
ideas.customer: Homeowners with cracked foundations or water entering basements or crawl spaces; partner customers are licensed repair crews needing more leads.
ideas.problem: Foundation cracks and water intrusion create urgent worries, while specialist crews may rely on word of mouth for leads.
ideas.offer: Market the service, schedule inspections, handle the sales conversation, and refer booked work to licensed crews.

pricing.model: The business keeps a piece of each job it brings to partner crews.

price_points.label: Common job range stated by the host

pricing.notes: The host does not state the lead operator's commission or share.

acquisition_channels.details: Set up a Google Business Profile and use before-and-after photos; the host says this can help stand out against crews relying on word of mouth.

quote.text: So, you know, a Google Business Profile, some before-and-after photos, and then just being by the phone when someone calls
quote.speaker: Host (name not stated)

ideas.delivery: The operator handles marketing, inspection scheduling, and the sales conversation. Licensed partner crews bring their equipment and perform the repair work.
unit_economics_claims: The host says jobs commonly run $5,000–$15,000, but does not state the lead operator's share.
ideas.startup_cost: The host describes startup needs as limited because partner crews own the specialized equipment; exact costs are not stated.

acquisition.how: A local listing and search visibility can bring inbound enquiries, with human response needed to convert urgent homeowner calls.

onboarding.how: Forms and scheduling can be automated, but symptoms and inspection details need human review.

delivery.how: The operator coordinates work remotely, but crews must inspect and repair the physical property.

billing.how: Commission invoicing could be automated after job completion, but the job value and partner share need confirmation.

support.how: Automated updates can handle routine scheduling, but homeowners with urgent property problems need human support.

uk_applicability.notes: Foundation and water problems also create demand in the UK, and the remote lead-coordination model could transfer. Local building practices, consumer protections, and subcontractor requirements may differ.

risks: The jobs are mostly one-off, so the business needs a continuing flow of new leads.
The operator depends on partner crews to complete work well.
Homeowners may expect a prompt response because the problem feels urgent.

quotes.text: You partner with licensed foundation waterproofing crews who already own all of that specialized equipment.
quotes.speaker: Host (name not stated)

ideas.name: Remote cleaning
ideas.one_liner: Market residential cleaning, hire independent cleaners to do the work, and retain a share of each job.
ideas.business_model: One-off deep cleans that can convert into recurring weekly, fortnightly, or monthly cleaning, with the operator and cleaner splitting job revenue.
ideas.customer: Busy two-income families searching for house cleaning.
ideas.problem: Customers need reliable home cleaning, while many local operators and solo cleaners do not answer calls, have websites, or actively grow.
ideas.offer: Generate cleaning enquiries, answer and schedule jobs, recruit independent cleaners with their own supplies and cars, pay them half the job revenue, and retain the other half.

pricing.model: Per-cleaning fee, with a stated 50/50 split between the operator and cleaner.

price_points.label: Cleaner share; operator keeps the other 50%

pricing.notes: The host presents the $350 deep clean and split as examples, not a guaranteed market price.

acquisition_channels.details: The host says busy families actively search Google for 'house cleaning near me.'

quote.text: And there's tons of busy two-income families that are actively searching for house cleaning near me in Google.
quote.speaker: Host (name not stated)

acquisition_channels.details: The host recommends a Google Business Profile and before-and-after photos as basic setup for the business.

quote.text: All you need to get started is really just your time, a laptop, and a couple cleaners.
quote.speaker: Host (name not stated)

ideas.delivery: Independent cleaners bring their own skills, supplies, and cars, then clean customers' homes. The operator handles marketing, sales, scheduling, and paying the cleaners.
unit_economics_claims: The host claims roughly one in three one-time cleanings converts to recurring service.
In an example, a $350 deep clean pays the cleaner $175, leaving the operator the other half before other costs.
The host says 25 recurring clients could produce close to $10,000 per month.
He says 30 cleans could produce about $10,000 monthly revenue or $3,000–$4,000 profit, with no employees.
ideas.startup_cost: The host says the business needs time, a laptop, and a couple of cleaners; exact cash costs are not stated.
ideas.time_to_first_revenue: Not stated for starting alone. The host's paid support offer claims it can help a client make a first sale within 21 days.

acquisition.how: Search visibility and a local profile can generate inbound leads, but calls and sales conversations need prompt human attention.

onboarding.how: Booking forms and reminders can be automated, with human review needed for scope, access, and cleaner availability.

delivery.how: The operator can coordinate remotely, but cleaners must physically clean each home.

billing.how: Online booking, payment collection, cleaner payouts, and recurring billing can be automated with occasional exception handling.

support.how: Routine confirmations and reminders can be automated, but complaints, access problems, and quality issues require human judgment.

uk_applicability.notes: Residential cleaning and local search demand transfer well to the UK. The host's claims about independent contractor status, workers' compensation, and payroll taxes are US-specific; UK worker-status, tax, and insurance obligations need separate treatment.

risks: The business depends on cleaner reliability and quality.
The host warns that owners undermine the model when they start cleaning jobs themselves and become reluctant to recruit.
The stated 50/50 split and profit examples do not account for all possible costs.
UK employment status and insurance rules may differ from the host's US assumptions.

evidence_quality.rationale: This is a promotional host-led ranking rather than a documented operator interview. It combines broad market claims, hypothetical examples, and at least one second-hand recruiting claim; most figures are not supported with named sources or detailed cost calculations.
evidence_quality.promotional_conflict: The host promotes his own full-length remote-cleaning training and one-to-one business support, describing a low-cost alternative to a franchise and making first-sale, client, revenue, and profit guarantee claims.
